lines.s: # Installed under many hook names: print the name, the arguments and the standard input.
# The same script under every client-side name of interest, and four names on the server:
cd .git/hooks && for h in prepare-commit-msg commit-msg post-commit pre-merge-commit post-merge
post-checkout pre-rebase post-rewrite pre-push; do cp pre-commit $h; done; cd ../..
for h in pre-receive update post-receive post-update; do cp .git/hooks/pre-commit

slides.body: Today you watched Git call a program at every gate, and predicted which gates can stop.

beats.text: A team wrote a hook: a program that Git runs by itself at a fixed point of a command. It works. Stage a private key, run git commit to save a snapshot, and the commit is refused. And yet a key is in the history of main.
beats.tele: A team wrote a hook: a program that Git runs by itself at a fixed point of a command. It works. Stage a private key, run `git commit` to save a snapshot, and the commit is refused. And yet a key is in the history of `main`.

beats.text: How did it get there? Several ways, and none of them needs bad intent. The commit was made by a rebase or a revert, which on Git 2.55 don't run pre-commit. Or the author deleted the file from disk and committed again, and a hook that checks the disk instead of the index was satisfied. Or the author's clone never had the hook installed. Or the author typed one extra option: --no-verify.
beats.tele: How did it get there? Several ways, and none of them needs bad intent. The commit was made by a rebase or a revert, which on Git 2.55 don't run `pre-commit`. Or the author deleted the file from disk and committed again, and a hook that checks the disk instead of the index was satisfied. Or the author's clone never had the hook installed. Or the author typed one extra option: `--no-verify`.

You've used the things hooks attach to: commit, merge, rebase, checkout, push. Today you watch Git call a program at each of those points.

beats.text: In one sentence: a hook is an executable file with a fixed name in the hooks directory, or, since Git 2.54, a command named in configuration, that Git runs at a defined point of a command, passing information as arguments and standard input. For some hooks, a non-zero exit status means "stop". The exit status is the number a program returns when it ends, and zero means success.

For some hooks, a non-zero exit status means "stop". The exit status is the number a program returns when it ends, and zero means success.

beats.text: Now precisely. The hooks manual lists 28 hook names. Git looks for them in $GIT_DIR/hooks, or in the directory named by core.hooksPath, and ignores files without the executable bit. A hook runs at the top of the working tree, the directory of files you edit, with GIT_DIR and related variables exported. git init copies inactive samples from the template directory.

beats.text: For each hook, four facts matter: which command runs it, what it receives as arguments and on standard input, whether a non-zero exit stops the command, and what skips it.

beats.text: On the server side, git receive-pack runs pre-receive once per push before any ref is updated, update once per pushed ref, and post-receive and post-update afterwards. A ref is a name such as a branch. Nothing on the client skips those hooks. An all-zero object ID in these inputs means "does not exist": the ref is being created, on the old side, or deleted, on the new side.

A ref is a name such as a branch. Nothing on the client skips those hooks. An all-zero object ID in these inputs means "does not exist": the ref is being created, on the old side, or deleted, on the new side.

beats.text: Three design rules for hooks you write.
beats.tele: Three design rules for hooks you write.

beats.text: Rule one. A commit is made from the index, so a pre-commit hook reads the index, not the files on disk. That means git diff --cached for content, and git cat-file -s on the staged path for sizes.
beats.tele: Rule one. A commit is made from the index, so a `pre-commit` hook reads the index, not the files on disk. That means `git diff --cached` for content, and `git cat-file -s` on the staged path for sizes.

beats.text: Rule two. A "pre" hook that can stop should be fast. The textbook's sentence is: use client-side hooks for fast feedback to the person at the keyboard, and keep them fast, or people learn the bypass.
beats.tele: Rule two. A "pre" hook that can stop should be fast. The textbook's sentence is: use client-side hooks for fast feedback to the person at the keyboard, and keep them fast, or people learn the bypass.

beats.text: Rule three. A hook is a program on a machine you don't control. If it needs a tool, it must check that the tool is there, and decide what a missing tool means. The same care goes for its exit status. A post-checkout hook can't undo a switch, but its exit status becomes the status of the command, so a failing hook breaks scripts that test git switch.
beats.tele: Rule three. A hook is a program on a machine you don't control. If it needs a tool, it must check that the tool is there, and decide what a missing tool means. The same care goes for its exit status. A `post-checkout` hook can't undo a switch, but its exit status becomes the status of the command, so a failing hook breaks scripts that test `git switch`.

beats.text: And when should you not rely on a hook? Whenever the check must hold for everyone. A hook that "checks every commit" checks the commits made by git commit and git merge. That's the subject of the next video.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy: tripwires in your own workshop. You place them. They do nothing in a colleague's workshop. And you can step over them.

beats.text: The analogy fits client-side hooks. It breaks for server-side ones, which sit at the door that every delivery must pass.

beats.text: Keep the two kinds apart for the rest of the course. A tripwire gives fast feedback to the person in the workshop. A check at the door is the only thing that inspects every delivery.

beats.text: It prints its own name, its arguments and, for some hooks, its standard input, and exits with 0. Your first prediction: how many hooks does a plain git commit -m run, and in which order? Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: Four, in this order: pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit. prepare-commit-msg received the message file and the word "message": it learned that the message came from -m.
beats.tele: Four, in this order: `pre-commit`, `prepare-commit-msg`, `commit-msg`, `post-commit`. `prepare-commit-msg` received the message file and the word "message": it learned that the message came from `-m`.

beats.text: The same four, and then post-rewrite with the argument amend, and on standard input the old commit ID and the new one.
beats.tele: The same four, and then `post-rewrite` with the argument `amend`, and on standard input the old commit ID and the new one.

beats.text: Two IDs, because an amend writes a new commit that takes the place of the old one.
beats.tele: Two IDs, because an amend writes a new commit that takes the place of the old one.

beats.text: post-checkout receives the previous HEAD, meaning where you were, the new HEAD and a flag. Creating a branch doesn't change the commit, so both IDs are equal. Restoring a file from a commit is a "file checkout": the flag is 0.
beats.tele: `post-checkout` receives the previous HEAD, meaning where you were, the new HEAD and a flag. Creating a branch doesn't change the commit, so both IDs are equal. Restoring a file from a commit is a "file checkout": the flag is 0.

beats.text: A merge runs pre-merge-commit in place of pre-commit, and post-merge at the end.
beats.tele: A merge runs `pre-merge-commit` in place of `pre-commit`, and `post-merge` at the end.

beats.text: Now a rebase that replays one commit, which means it makes a copy with a new ID. Do pre-commit and commit-msg run for the replayed commit? Predict. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Now a rebase that replays one commit, which means it makes a copy with a new ID. Do `pre-commit` and `commit-msg` run for the replayed commit? Predict. I'll wait.

beats.text: They don't. pre-rebase ran once and post-rewrite once.
beats.tele: They don't. `pre-rebase` ran once and `post-rewrite` once.

beats.text: For the replayed commit, prepare-commit-msg and post-commit ran. pre-commit and commit-msg didn't. If you expected them to run, that's normal. The textbook adds that git revert, which adds a commit that undoes another, behaves the same on Git 2.55. This is the first answer to our opening question.
beats.tele: For the replayed commit, `prepare-commit-msg` and `post-commit` ran. `pre-commit` and `commit-msg` didn't. If you expected them to run, that's normal. The textbook adds that `git revert`, which adds a commit that undoes another, behaves the same on Git 2.55. This is the first answer to our opening question.

beats.text: pre-push ran in your clone, with the remote name and URL as arguments and one line for the ref on standard input. The remote ID is all zeros because the branch is new there.
beats.tele: `pre-push` ran in your clone, with the remote name and URL as arguments and one line for the ref on standard input. The remote ID is all zeros because the branch is new there.

beats.text: The lines that start with "remote:" were printed by hooks in the other repository and sent back: pre-receive, update, post-receive, post-update.
beats.tele: The lines that start with "remote:" were printed by hooks in the other repository and sent back: `pre-receive`, `update`, `post-receive`, `post-update`.

beats.text: Check your paper. --no-verify skipped pre-commit and commit-msg.

beats.text: prepare-commit-msg and post-commit still ran. Of these two, prepare-commit-msg can still stop a commit by exiting non-zero, with or without --no-verify. The textbook confirmed that by a run on Git 2.55.0.

beats.text: This hook looks at what is staged: git diff --cached for a private-key header, and the size of each staged file. Now a deploy key and a 600 kilobyte checkpoint are staged together with a real change.
beats.tele: This hook looks at what is staged: `git diff --cached` for a private-key header, and the size of each staged file. Now a deploy key and a 600 kilobyte checkpoint are staged together with a real change.

beats.text: Two messages on standard error, exit status 1, no commit. Now the developer deletes the two files from disk and tries again. Quick quiz: does the commit go through now, or is it refused again? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Two messages on standard error, exit status 1, no commit. Now the developer deletes the two files from disk and tries again. Quick quiz: does the commit go through now, or is it refused again? Say it out loud.

beats.text: Refused again. The hook reads the index, and the files are still staged. Only after git restore --staged does the commit go through.
beats.tele: Refused again. The hook reads the index, and the files are still staged. Only after `git restore --staged` does the commit go through.

beats.text: On disk, deploy_key is gone. In the index it's still staged. A hook that had looked at the disk would have let the key into the commit. That's the index, paid off. Know the limits of this hook, though: file names without spaces only, one secret pattern, and one option removes it.

beats.text: Exit status 0. The key is committed.
beats.tele: Exit status 0. The key is committed.

beats.text: Refused, with the expected form and the subject it got. Then look at git status -s: the change shows as unstaged. git commit -a stages into a temporary index and discards it when the commit fails. The lab also shows the classic defect of such hooks. They refuse the subjects that Git writes itself, "Merge branch" and "fixup!", and a merge then stops half-way.

beats.text: The push is refused before anything is sent, and the hook names the unfinished commit. main is still two ahead.
beats.tele: The push is refused before anything is sent, and the hook names the unfinished commit. `main` is still two ahead.

beats.text: The hook uses its three arguments: it exits at once for a file checkout, and compares the lock file between the old and the new HEAD.
beats.tele: The hook uses its three arguments: it exits at once for a file checkout, and compares the lock file between the old and the new HEAD.

beats.text: The pull was a fast-forward, with no merge commit, and post-merge ran all the same. Now the exit status.
beats.tele: The pull was a fast-forward, with no merge commit, and `post-merge` ran all the same. Now the exit status.

beats.text: The hook exited with 3, git switch exited with 1, and the branch was switched. Think of a hook that calls a tool which isn't installed on this machine. The command "fails", the switch has happened, and every script that tests the status of git switch breaks. That's why a hook that depends on tools must check for them, and exit 0 with a message when they're missing.

That's why a hook that depends on tools must check for them, and exit 0 with a message when they're missing.

beats.text: It counts the commits to be rebased, and the ones among them that no remote-tracking branch contains.
beats.tele: It counts the commits to be rebased, and the ones among them that no remote-tracking branch contains.

beats.text: A remote-tracking branch records where a branch was on the server. If the numbers differ, some are published.
beats.tele: A remote-tracking branch records where a branch was on the server. If the numbers differ, some are published.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: A pre-commit hook that inspects files on disk. Root cause: a commit is made from the index; what is staged can differ from what is on disk in both directions.
beats.tele: A `pre-commit` hook that inspects files on disk. Root cause: a commit is made from the index; what is staged can differ from what is on disk in both directions.

beats.text: Believing a pre-commit or commit-msg hook checks every commit. Root cause: on Git 2.55 the commits replayed by a rebase, and those made by a revert, run neither.
beats.tele: Believing a `pre-commit` or `commit-msg` hook checks every commit. Root cause: on Git 2.55 the commits replayed by a rebase, and those made by a revert, run neither.

beats.text: A commit-msg pattern that rejects Git's own subjects. Root cause: merges and fixup commits have generated subjects, and the hook stops a merge half-way.
beats.tele: A `commit-msg` pattern that rejects Git's own subjects. Root cause: merges and fixup commits have generated subjects, and the hook stops a merge half-way.

beats.text: A post-checkout hook that exits non-zero when a tool is missing. Root cause: its exit status becomes the status of git switch although the switch has happened.
beats.tele: A `post-checkout` hook that exits non-zero when a tool is missing. Root cause: its exit status becomes the status of `git switch` although the switch has happened.

beats.text: A slow "pre" hook. Root cause: it runs at every commit for the person at the keyboard; people learn --no-verify, and then no check runs at all.
beats.tele: A slow "pre" hook. Root cause: it runs at every commit for the person at the keyboard; people learn `--no-verify`, and then no check runs at all.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. An ML platform team installs four hooks in its service repositories. A pre-commit that checks staged content for key headers and for files above a size limit, with a message that points to Git LFS or the data store. A commit-msg hook for the subject convention, which lets through the subjects that Git writes itself.

A `pre-commit` that checks staged content for key headers and for files above a size limit, with a message that points to Git LFS or the data store. beats.text: A post-checkout and post-merge pair that says when the dependency lock file changed, and that exits 0 with a note when the comparison can't be made. And a pre-push guard that keeps commits whose subject starts with WIP off main.
